column2: Chain · Crossing IV, between the two zones.
Silence
Gnosis: To Know Is to Remember
Gnosis is neither belief nor works. It is knowledge — the kind one has of a beloved face, not of a formula.
“Who we were, what we have become; where we were, where we have been thrown; where we are hurrying, what we are freed from.” (Theodotus)
“Whoever does not know himself knows nothing; whoever knows himself already knows the depth of the All.” (Book of Thomas the Contender)
That is why Silence is the most dangerous Aeon: one cannot remember what has been erased.
But the spark does not forget. It only waits for someone to ask its name.
Excerpts from Theodotus 78,2; Book of Thomas the Contender (NHC II,7, 138); Gospel of Truth (NHC I,3).
Silence · Crossing I, among the first empty shelves.
Nag Hammadi, 1945
For more than fifteen hundred years, nearly everything known about the Gnostics came from their opponents.
In December 1945, near Nag Hammadi, in Egypt, the farmer Muhammad Ali al-Samman was digging for fertilizer at the foot of a cliff and found a jar.
Inside: twelve papyrus codices bound in leather, and leaves of a thirteenth, copied in Coptic in the fourth century.
Fifty-two treatises. The Apocryphon of John. The Gospel of Thomas. The Gospel of Truth. The Hypostasis of the Archons.
It is said that some leaves ended up in the household oven before anyone knew what they were.
An entire library lay silent in the earth for sixteen centuries. And even so, it spoke.
James M. Robinson (ed.), The Nag Hammadi Library in English (1977), introduction.
Silence · The Challenge, at the Champion's shrine.
The Apocryphon of John
It is the whole myth, from the One to humankind, told as a revelation to John, son of Zebedee.
It survived in four copies — three at Nag Hammadi, one in a Berlin codex — a sign that it was widely read.
In it the Savior tells of Yaldabaoth's origin, the names of the Archons, the making of Adam and the chain of Fate.
It teaches that the soul that does not know is born again, from prison to prison, until it wakes; and it ends with a hymn: “Rise, and remember.”
Something very close to it was already circulating around 180: Irenaeus summarizes its myth in order to refute it. The refutation helped preserve it.
The blank pages of this Aeon are what would remain without the jar. Read while you can.
NHC II,1; III,1; IV,1; Berlin Codex (BG 8502,2); Irenaeus, Against Heresies I,29.
Silence · Crossing V, before Yabel's antechamber.
Mirror
Pistis Sophia and the Repentances
There is a book in which Sophia, fallen into chaos, sings thirteen repentances.
Below her she saw a light — the lion-faced power of the Arrogant One — and took it for the Light above. She went down after it.
The powers of chaos closed around her. She sang: “O Light of lights, in whom I trusted from the beginning, hear my repentance.”
After each song, a disciple — often Mary Magdalene — answers with a psalm that interprets it.
Sophia is not saved by strength. She is saved by remembering whom to call.
This Aeon's Mirror is that false light seen from above. The reflection is not the Light. It never was.
Pistis Sophia (Askew Codex, 3rd–4th c.), books I–II.
Mirror · Crossing I, past the still waters.
Valentinus and Basilides
Not all Gnostics were anonymous. Two masters taught in Alexandria and in Rome, in the second century.
Hippolytus says Basilides spoke of a God who “is not,” so far beyond being that not even “exists” can be said of him. Irenaeus says the heavens numbered 365.
Valentinus, poet and teacher, hoped to become bishop of Rome, Tertullian reports. His school carried the myth of Sophia across the Mediterranean.
For the Valentinians there were three natures: matter, which dissolves; soul, which chooses; spirit, which returns.
They wrote commentaries, psalms, letters and homilies — almost all of it lost.
What we know of them is a reflection in the words of those who fought them. Even so, it shines.
Irenaeus I,1–8 and I,24; Hippolytus, Refutation VII,20–27; Clement, Stromata; Tertullian, Against the Valentinians 4.
Mirror · Crossing IV, past the shrine.
Blight
The Gospel of Thomas
“These are the hidden words that Jesus, the living one, spoke, and that Didymus Judas Thomas set down.”
One hundred and fourteen sayings. No birth, no miracles, no passion: only the voice, and the ear of whoever understands. Whether it is Gnostic, scholars debate.
“The Kingdom is within you and around you. Know yourselves, and you will be known.”
“If you bring to light what is within you, it will save you. If you lack it, its lack will kill you.”
“The Father's Kingdom lies spread across the earth, and people do not see it.”
In the Blight, everything rots on the outside. Thomas's saying asks what rots on the inside.
Gospel of Thomas (NHC II,2), sayings 1, 3, 70 and 113.
Blight · Crossing I, just past the swamp.
The Hymn of the Pearl
A prince of the East is sent down to Egypt to fetch a pearl guarded by a serpent.
His parents take from him his robe of light and promise: “When you return with the pearl, you will wear it again.”
In Egypt he eats their food, wears their clothes — and forgets. He forgets the pearl, forgets the king, forgets who he is.
Then a letter flies to him like an eagle: “Wake, and rise from your sleep. Remember you are a child of kings. Remember the pearl.”
He wakes, charms the serpent with his father's name, takes the pearl and climbs. The robe comes to meet him, and he recognizes himself in it.
The poison of this swamp is the food of Egypt. The letter is anything that makes you remember.
Acts of Thomas 108–113 (the “Hymn of the Pearl,” in Syriac, 2nd–3rd c.).
Blight · Crossing IV, past the shrine.
Crown
The Call and the Awakening
The texts agree on one point: the spark does not wake on its own. Something calls it.
“Rise, and remember,” says the hymn of the Apocryphon of John. “Wake,” says the letter of the Pearl. The call echoes among Mandaeans and Manichaeans too.
“Whoever has gnosis, when called, hears, answers, and turns toward the one who calls,” says the Gospel of Truth.
The Call comes from outside the Kenoma: from an envoy in disguise, from a letter, from a pain that breaks the spell.
The one who calls cannot climb for you. The true Call awakens, and lets go.
The Crown of this Aeon awaits a king. The Awakening waits for no one to sit.
Apocryphon of John (NHC II,1, 30–31, the hymn of Providence); Gospel of Truth (NHC I,3, 21–22); Acts of Thomas 110.
Crown · Crossing I, past the empty thrones.
Docetism: The Apparent Body
Some groups taught that the Savior lived among humans only in appearance — dokein, in Greek, “to seem.”
Basilides, according to Irenaeus, said another was crucified in his place; the Nag Hammadi Apocalypse of Peter shows him laughing above the cross.
Others disagreed fiercely: if he did not truly suffer, what did he truly save? Not every Gnostic was a docetist.
The dispute lasted centuries, and one need not take sides to hear it.
It asks what this Aeon asks: if the body is appearance, why is the pain so real?
The body reading this stone bleeds. Perhaps the answer lies in the blood.
Irenaeus I,24,4 (Basilides); Second Treatise of the Great Seth (NHC VII,2, 56); Apocalypse of Peter (NHC VII,3, 81–83).
Crown · Crossing IV, between the two zones.
The Center
Salvation as Return
For the Gnostic, salvation is neither pardon nor prize. It is return — restoration — of every spark to the Fullness.
Sophia, remembering, is received back. And the blind son? For the Valentinians, he rises to his mother's place; On the Origin of the World casts him into the abyss.
“Have you found the beginning, that you now seek the end? Where the beginning is, the end will be,” says the Gospel of Thomas.
No one returns alone: the Call goes out to those still sleeping, one by one, until the Kenoma is emptied.
Here in the Center there is no voice, no throne, no crown. Only the way back.
Choosing how to return — to rise, to sit or to sow — was never any god's to decide.
Gospel of Thomas 18; Irenaeus I,7,1; On the Origin of the World (NHC II,5, 126–127); Tripartite Tractate (NHC I,5).
